docs.title: Home
docs.text:
EmbAI is a Windows desktop application. It does not replace Keil — firmware is still compiled by your local Keil MDK and flashed over J-Link/ST-Link. What EmbAI takes over is the part that actually eats your day: writing code, digging through datasheets, assigning pins, watching waveforms, and iterating on display UIs.

Before you start

You need Keil MDK and the J-Link drivers installed — they are required for building and flashing, and EmbAI does not bundle them. See Install & Setup.

docs.title: EmbAI
docs.text:
An AI-driven STM32 firmware development environment. The wizard generates a project skeleton that compiles; the AI writes the actual firmware, file by file, from your schematic and your requirements.

Download for Windows Quick Start

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Projects grow out of a conversation

    After the 6-step wizard settles the chip, firmware library, RTOS and peripherals, the AI panel opens and starts asking you what the firmware should actually do — then writes it one file at a time. Existing Keil projects can be migrated in wholesale.

    Projects

  • An AI assistant with plans and approvals

    Around 130 tools covering file edits, build and flash, breakpoints and stepping, register reads, pin configuration and Git. In Plan mode the AI submits a plan for your approval first; the approval mode decides what it must ask about.

    AI Assistant

  • Tune a display without a board

    Your OLED/TFT driver code is compiled and run natively on your PC. The SPI/I²C command stream is intercepted and rendered onto a canvas — 22 controllers supported. When it looks right, promote it to hardware.

    Virtual Display

  • Feed the schematic to the AI

    Upload a schematic PDF or image and the AI extracts components, nets and MCU pin mappings. After that, @schematic: references it in chat. Datasheets work the same way — ask how a register should be configured and get an answer with page citations.

    Schematics & Knowledge

  • Serial, beyond a text console

    Besides the ordinary serial terminal there is a drag-and-drop dashboard: waveforms, gauges, numeric readouts, indicators, sliders and buttons. FireWater / JustFloat / RawData protocols, with auto-detection.

    Serial & Dashboard

  • Full debugging and visualisation

    Breakpoints, stepping, variables, call stack, memory read/write, expression evaluation, target power control. Plus pin configurator, clock tree, peripheral block diagram, memory map, DMA channels and NVIC priorities.

    Debugging

docs.title: Supported
docs.text: OS Windows 10 / 11 (64-bit) Chips 787 STM32 parts across 18 series Firmware libraries HAL, LL, HAL+LL, Standard Peripheral Library (SPL) RTOS Bare metal, FreeRTOS, RT-Thread, CMSIS-RTOS Toolchain Keil MDK (UV4) — currently the only supported firmware compiler Debug probes J-Link, ST-Link, DAPLink / CMSIS-DAP, and serial ISP

docs.title: Install & Setup
docs.text:
EmbAI currently ships for Windows 10 / 11 (64-bit) only.

Installing EmbAI itself is not enough — building and flashing depend on two third-party tools you have to install yourself.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Required? Used for EmbAI installer Yes The application Keil MDK Yes The only firmware toolchain J-Link drivers Yes Flashing and debugging always go through J-Link — see section 3 GitHub access Yes, for the first project Downloading the HAL/CMSIS firmware library OpenOCD Optional Needed when flashing over ST-Link CMake + GCC Optional Only used by the Virtual Display

docs.title: 1. Install EmbAI
docs.text:
Download the installer from the Releases page and run it.

You don't need to download later versions manually: click the version number at the top left of the app → Check for updates to download and install in place.

docs.title: 2. Install Keil MDK
docs.text:
Download MDK from the Arm Keil site and follow their instructions for installation and licensing.

EmbAI looks for UV4.exe in this order and uses the first hit:

  1. keil_path in the project's .embai/config.json
  2. The Keil path stored in application settings (Settings → Compiler)
  3. The KEIL_PATH environment variable
  4. Default install locations C:\Keil_v5\UV4\UV4.exe and C:\Keil\UV4\UV4.exe
  5. The registry and PATH

A default installation normally needs no configuration at all.

Build says UV4.exe was not found

未找到 Keil UV4.exe。请在「环境检测」中配置 Keil 路径，
或设置 KEIL_PATH 环境变量 / 在 .embai/config.json 写入 keil_path。
Set the path manually as described in section 4.

docs.title: 3. Install probe drivers
docs.text:
J-Link (default)ST-LinkDAPLink / CMSIS-DAPSerial ISP

Install SEGGER's J-Link Software and Documentation Pack. EmbAI talks to the probe through its JLinkARM.dll.

Afterwards the J-Link indicator in the toolbar should detect your probe. If it doesn't, you can point EmbAI at the DLL manually from environment detection.

The ST-Link path requires OpenOCD. Install it yourself and make sure openocd is on your PATH.

Target series covered: F0 / F1 / F2 / F3 / F4 / F7 / G0 / G4 / H7 / L0 / L1 / L4 / L5 / U5 / WB / WL.

Not available in release builds

This path depends on the Python pyocd package, which is not shipped with the installer (it is in neither backend/requirements.txt nor the packaging spec). The new-project wizard lets you select DAPLink, but connecting fails immediately with pyocd not available.

The released backend is a frozen bundle with its own interpreter, so pip install pyocd into your system Python does not help either. Use J-Link or ST-Link for now.

With no debug probe at all, some parts can be flashed over the serial bootloader (BOOT0 pulled high).

The probe type can only be chosen in step 5 of the new-project wizard, which writes it to .embai/config.json; there is no way to change it from inside the application afterwards. The J-Link indicator in the toolbar opens J-Link settings — interface, speed, reset type and other J-Link-specific parameters — not a probe-type selector.

Flashing and debugging always go through J-Link today

The probe chosen in step 5 currently only affects the generated project configuration; EmbAI's own flash/debug path always uses the J-Link backend. To flash over ST-Link or DAPLink, use those vendors' own tools for the time being.

docs.title: 4. Environment detection
docs.text:
Settings (gear icon, top right) → Compiler → Open environment detection.

This dialog probes for Keil, J-Link, ARM GCC, CMake, Ninja, OpenOCD, Python and Git, and marks whether the required ones are present. The Keil and J-Link rows have a Configure path button that lets you point at UV4.exe / JLinkARM.dll directly; the choice is saved immediately.

The GCC and CMake paths on the Compiler page do not affect firmware builds

Firmware is compiled by Keil only. Those two entries currently play no part in it.

docs.title: 5. Networking: the first project downloads a firmware library
docs.text:
When you create a project, EmbAI fetches the matching HAL/CMSIS sources for your chip series from the STM32Cube repositories on GitHub. This runs in the background with progress in the status bar.

  • Building before it finishes is blocked with a "firmware library not ready" message — just wait.
  • On failure the status bar shows Retry and Ignore.
  • On networks where GitHub is slow or blocked, configure a proxy before creating a project.

docs.title: 6. Optional: the virtual display toolchain
docs.text:
The Virtual Display compiles and runs your driver code natively on your PC, so it needs a host CMake and GCC — not a cross toolchain.

When they are missing, /virtual/build returns HTTP 424 and a banner appears in that view.

Install the toolchain manually rather than relying on the one-click button

The one-click installer downloads and unpacks a toolchain, but its bundled checksums are placeholders, so integrity verification is skipped entirely — whatever is downloaded gets installed unverified. Install CMake and MinGW-w64 / LLVM-mingw yourself, add them to PATH, and reopen the view.

docs.title: 7. Where files live
docs.text: Location Contents <project>\.embai\ Per-project configuration (config.json), dashboard layout (dashboard.json) %USERPROFILE%\.embai\ Local database, firmware-pack / Pack / toolchain caches, file history, uploads, and the crash log embai_crash.log %APPDATA%\EmbAI\ The desktop runtime log backend.log. This is what Help & feedback attaches

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom What to do Blank window or stuck splash after install Give it a few seconds, then restart. If it persists, use Help & Feedback — logs are attached automatically Build can't find UV4.exe See section 2 J-Link indicator stays grey Check the SEGGER driver pack is installed, that the USB cable carries data, and that the board is powered ST-Link doesn't work Make sure openocd is on your PATH Firmware library download keeps failing Requires GitHub access; set a proxy and press Retry in the status bar Virtual display reports a missing toolchain Install CMake + GCC onto PATH, see section 6

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: From nothing to a successful flash. About 20 minutes, most of it spent waiting for Keil and the firmware library to download.

docs.title: 1. Install the two things EmbAI does not bundle
docs.text:
Required Why Keil MDK Firmware is compiled only by Keil's UV4.exe. EmbAI ships no compiler. J-Link drivers The default flash and debug path. For ST-Link or DAPLink see Install & Setup.

You also need internet access the first time you create a project — the HAL/CMSIS firmware library is fetched from the STM32Cube repositories on GitHub.

Installation and troubleshooting: Install & Setup.

docs.title: 2. Install EmbAI and sign in
docs.text:
1. Download the Windows installer from the Releases page, install and launch.
  2. The sign-in screen has exactly one button: Sign in / Register via browser. It opens your system browser; once you finish signing up or signing in there, you are returned to the app automatically.

Why the browser

Accounts, AI quota and credits are managed centrally in the cloud. Going through the browser lets you reuse an existing GitHub / Google / WeChat session and keeps password fields out of the app. See Account & Credits.

docs.title: 3. Confirm your environment
docs.text:
Settings (gear icon, top right) → Compiler → Open environment detection.

Keil and J-Link should both show as installed. If either is flagged, use Configure path on that row and point it at UV4.exe or JLinkARM.dll.

Don't skip this

If Keil is not configured you will not find out until you press Build: 未找到 Keil UV4.exe。请在「环境检测」中配置 Keil 路径……

docs.title: 4. Create a project
docs.text:
Click New project on the welcome screen (or New in the toolbar) and work through the 6 steps:

Step What you choose 1. Chip Filter by series or search a part number — 787 STM32 parts 2. Firmware library HAL / LL / HAL+LL / SPL, optionally pinning a Cube package version 3. RTOS Bare metal / FreeRTOS / RT-Thread / CMSIS-RTOS 4. Peripherals & middleware UART, SPI, I²C, TIM, ADC, DMA, configured individually 5. Toolchain & probe Defaults to Keil + J-Link + SWD + 4000 kHz 6. Name & location Plus sample code, Git init, unit tests, Doxygen

When the wizard finishes, don't build yet: watch the status bar. The firmware library is downloading from GitHub and the project is not ready until that progress bar completes. If it fails, the status bar offers a Retry button.

Building before the library is down

The build is blocked with a message saying the firmware library is not ready. That is deliberate — it stops you from compiling against missing HAL headers.

docs.title: 5. Let the AI write the firmware
docs.text:
The wizard only produces a skeleton that compiles. Once the project exists, the AI panel opens by itself and starts asking what the firmware should do (which LED, which UART, what baud rate), then generates the code one file at a time.

This is the intended workflow — you are not meant to start from an empty main.c.

To see its intent before it acts, turn on Plan mode (+ to the left of the input → Plan mode, or Ctrl+Alt+P): the AI submits a plan for approval before touching anything.

docs.title: 6. Build
docs.text:
Press Build in the toolbar. The bottom panel switches to Build output and streams Keil's log, ending in N Error(s), M Warning(s).

If it fails, just tell the AI to fix the build errors — it can read that output.

docs.title: 7. Connect a board and flash
docs.text:
With the probe connected, press Build & flash. A progress dialog walks through erase → program → verify.

  • If the probe is not connected yet, EmbAI connects automatically using the chip from the project configuration.
  • 未找到固件，请先构建项目 means nothing has been built successfully yet.
  • 自动连接失败 usually means no power, a locked debug port, or the wrong interface/speed.

On success the dialog offers Open serial port, which takes you straight to the next step.

docs.title: 8. Look at the output
docs.text:
Bottom panel → Serial terminal, pick the port and baud rate, connect. HEX view, timestamps and RX/TX byte counters are all available.

If your firmware streams numbers rather than text, try Serial Dashboard in the activity bar — a few waveforms and gauges beat staring at a screen of digits. See Serial & Dashboard.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:

  • Debugging — breakpoints, stepping, variables
  • Virtual Display — build an OLED/TFT UI with no board on your desk
  • AI Assistant — Plan mode, approval modes, @ references to schematics and datasheets

docs.title: Common sticking points
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix Build says it can't find UV4.exe Keil missing or unconfigured. Settings → Compiler → Open environment detection → Configure path "Please open a project first" No project is open — create or open one Firmware library not ready Wait for the status-bar progress; on failure press Retry Firmware library never downloads Requires GitHub access. Fix networking or set a proxy, then retry Flashing reports auto-connect failure Check power and wiring; try JTAG instead of SWD, or a lower speed GCC / CMake paths set under Compiler do nothing Firmware builds only use Keil; those entries do not affect it

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: This page explains what each part of the window is for; the individual features are covered in the sub-pages. If you haven't installed yet, start with Install & Setup; to run through everything once, see Quick Start.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
The window has five parts:

Area Position Contents Toolbar Top Version, project name, build/flash buttons, hardware indicators, AI, settings, avatar Activity bar Far left Entry points for each view, grouped by purpose Main area Centre The current view (editor, debugger, pin configurator, …) AI assistant Right Docked panel, Ctrl+J to toggle, survives view switches Bottom panel Bottom Serial terminal / RTT log / Build output Status bar Last line Project path, Git status, cursor position, firmware download progress, probe state

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text:
• Version number (right of the logo) — opens the About box, and is where Check for updates lives
  • Project name — switch project, create one, migrate a Keil project, or open by path
  • New / Build / Flash / Build & flash — the four main actions
  • J-Link and Serial indicators — connection state; click to open settings or connect/disconnect

docs.title: Activity bar groups
docs.text:
Group Views Core Editor, Debug, Source control (plus global search, Ctrl+Shift+F) Hardware Pin configurator, Clock tree Build analysis Map file analysis Chip visualisation Peripheral block diagram, Memory map, DMA channels, NVIC priorities J-Link J-Scope waveform (a demo placeholder — not wired to real data) Serial Serial dashboard Packs Pack installer, Pack details Virtual & schematics Virtual display, Schematics, Coding standard, Project knowledge base

Three items are pinned at the bottom: AI assistant, Settings, Help & feedback.

The activity bar can be collapsed, leaving only the Core group and whichever group is active.

docs.title: Status bar
docs.text: Left to right: project path · Git branch and change count (click to open source control) · current file · firmware library download progress (with retry/ignore) · Ln x, Col y · J-Link state · Serial state.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text:
• Projects

    The 6-step new-project wizard, opening existing projects, migrating a Keil project in, and the recent-projects list.

  • Editor

    File tree, tabs, split view, global search, symbol navigation, inline AI chat, and the full keyboard shortcut reference.

  • Build & Flash

    How the Keil build runs, how to read the build output, the four flashing paths, and what the common failures mean.

  • Debugging

    Starting a session, breakpoints and watchpoints, stepping, variables and call stack, memory access, expression evaluation, target power control.

  • Serial & Dashboard

    Connection parameters and HEX view in the terminal; the dashboard's seven widgets, three data protocols and protocol auto-detection.

  • AI Assistant

    Built-in versus your own models, Plan mode, approval modes, attachments and @ references, slash commands, session management.

  • Virtual Display

    Iterate on an OLED/TFT UI with no hardware attached — 22 controllers, injected buttons and potentiometers, then promote to hardware.

  • Schematics & Knowledge

    Upload a schematic and let the AI extract the pin mapping, ask questions about datasheets, and enforce your team's coding standard.

  • Account & Credits

    Signing in, credit-based billing for built-in models, balance and top-ups, and what each billing error means.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Opened from the gear icon, with five pages:

Page Contents Account Current identity, credit balance, usage summary, top-up General Theme, language, autosave interval, editor font size, file encoding, system notifications Compiler Keil and probe paths, plus environment detection Git Commit identity and other Git settings AI models Built-in and custom models, API keys, web search, agent parameters, tool permissions

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text: Help & feedback at the bottom of the activity bar submits feedback directly to us, and can optionally attach a screenshot and recent logs (you see exactly what will be attached before sending, and can turn it off). You can also take the discussion to GitHub Issues.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
Scope of this page

Recent releases are documented here in English. Older entries (v0.1.73 and earlier) exist only in the Chinese changelog, which is the complete history.

docs.title: Features
docs.text: • The documentation site was rewritten, and an English edition added. The eight pages published until now were written for the first release and had not followed the product for more than three months. They described building with CMake + Ninja + arm-gcc, running on Windows/macOS/Linux, cloning the source, and pasting in your own API key — whereas EmbAI is a Windows desktop application whose firmware is compiled only by Keil MDK, installed from an installer, with cloud accounts. They also referenced things that do not exist in the code at all (an EMBAI_PORT variable, ~/.embai/settings.json, six invented AI tool names, three non-existent scripts) and contradicted themselves on endpoint paths. Everything is now rewritten from the code: a nine-chapter user guide organised by feature (projects, editor, build & flash, debugging, serial & dashboard, AI assistant, virtual display, schematics & knowledge, account & credits), Chinese at the original address and English under /en/ with a language switcher, styled to match the EmbAI brand. The architecture, development and API reference pages were retired — they had drifted badly out of date and were written for maintainers rather than users. The documentation cards in Help & feedback point at the new chapters.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• "Attach screenshot" was capturing the feedback panel itself. The capture takes the whole window, and the Help & feedback panel was sitting on top of it as an overlay with a dimming backdrop — so every attachment showed the feedback panel over a darkened background, hiding the AI assistant or editor state the user actually wanted to show. The panel is now hidden for the instant of the capture and restored immediately, with the text you have written, your checkbox choices and the fetched diagnostics all preserved.
  • Made it clear that the GitHub route pre-fills rather than submits. The button used to read "or file an issue on GitHub", sitting right under the "Submit feedback" button that really does send — but GitHub does not let an application file an issue on your behalf, so this path can only open a pre-filled form in your browser that you still have to submit yourself. The button text and the message shown after clicking now say so.
  • Fixed nothing happening when the GitHub button was pressed with a long body. The length limit on the pre-filled link was measured in characters, but Chinese is percent-encoded as UTF-8 in a URL at nine characters per glyph — a 1,200-character body produced an 11,431 character link, far past the system limit, so the browser never opened and nothing was reported. The limit is now applied to the actual link length (bodies up to roughly 145 Chinese characters are unaffected); longer ones pre-fill the beginning and say the full text is still in the input box. Failures to open the browser are now reported instead of ignored.
  • Screenshot failures are now reported instead of silently doing nothing.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • Help & feedback went from mock-up to a real feature. Previously all 12 links in the panel were dead placeholders, the video-tutorial durations and view counts were invented, "attach screenshot" was a toggle that sent nothing, and pressing "Submit feedback" only displayed "submitted successfully" — nothing was actually sent. Now the quick-start and documentation links point at the real online docs; feedback is genuinely submitted and visible server-side; failures report the actual reason and offer GitHub Issues instead of pretending to succeed; "attach screenshot" really captures the current window; and before submitting you are shown the version, OS and backend log tail that will be attached, with the log optional. The two non-existent entries (video tutorials and Discord) were removed.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• Tightened the capability boundary and timeout handling of AI delegated exploration. Sub-agents are now restricted to exactly three tools (list directory, search, read file) and no longer silently gain reach when new read-only tools are added elsewhere. Startup, execution, cancellation and cleanup share one five-minute budget, and a timeout returns the partial findings rather than nothing. Delegated exploration is no longer accounted as a write operation, so it neither holds the write lock nor triggers the "previous write result unknown" retry guard.
  • Removed AI tool switches that could not be turned off. The tool list now shows only tools you can actually enable or disable, omitting three built-ins whose switches had no effect.
  • Question cards could be lost when a turn was cancelled. If a turn was cancelled at the exact moment the AI asked you something, the question card is now still written to the transcript and survives a refresh.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • Reinstalling or updating sometimes required signing in again before models appeared. When the saved sign-in token had already expired at cold start, the local backend did not return 401, so the front end never refreshed it — but forwarding the expired token to the cloud to fetch the model list was rejected, leaving the list empty. Expired tokens are now refreshed before fetching, the model list is re-fetched after a successful refresh, and a failed cloud fetch retries after refreshing. No manual re-login needed.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • Fixed a crash loop with custom models in the packaged build. When the local encryption key changed and a saved custom-model API key could no longer be decrypted, the backend crashed and retried endlessly. It now reports clearly that the key cannot be decrypted and asks you to re-enter it in settings, while remaining fully usable — you can switch models and stop the turn. The local encryption key is no longer silently regenerated when it fails to load (which orphaned every stored key). A dropped AI connection now backs off exponentially and stops after repeated failures with a "Retry connection" button, instead of reconnecting every two seconds forever.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Light theme. Light, dark and follow-system appearances, switchable in settings. The editor, chat code blocks and project visualisation SVGs all follow; the dark appearance is unchanged.
  • Serial dashboard. Data visualisation for MCU serial debugging: waveform data is parsed live from the raw byte stream, with built-in support for common protocols (FireWater, JustFloat) and auto-detection. Waveform, numeric, gauge, LED, button and slider widgets can be arranged by hand — or you can ask the AI to build the whole panel from what your firmware prints.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• Fixed intermittent "ticket exchange failed" errors for new users on the packaged build. The AI runtime no longer starts on the backend's critical path; a momentary hiccup there can't drag down the whole backend and take sign-in and account endpoints with it. The backend and its health endpoint come up immediately, and the AI side retries in the background or loads lazily. Ticket exchange gained backoff retries and a longer timeout to cover the window right after startup. When the AI runtime exits unexpectedly, the real reason is now written to the backend log.
  • The reasoning-depth menu now scrolls instead of clipping the last options.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • Built-in, GLM and custom models no longer raise a "model metadata not found" runtime warning. Tool definitions are still delivered, the per-turn fallback warning is gone, and long conversations are no longer truncated below the real context limit. Routing and billing are unchanged.

docs.title: Signing in
docs.text:
The sign-in screen has one button: Sign in / Register via browser.

It opens your system browser, where you can register or sign in (email verification code, or GitHub / Google / WeChat), and returns you to the app when you're done.

The benefit is that you can reuse a third-party session you're already signed into, and the app never needs a password field.

The avatar menu at the top right has: Projects, Profile, Account & usage, Operation log, and Sign out.

docs.title: When credits are spent
docs.text:
Credits are consumed only by the built-in models. Models you configure yourself (Settings → AI models → My models) talk directly to the vendor and do not go through EmbAI billing.

Everything else — building, flashing, debugging, serial, virtual display — costs nothing.

docs.title: What the balance is made of
docs.text:
The balance has two buckets:

Bucket Source Granted Issued monthly according to your tier Purchased What you have topped up

Tiers are FREE / PRO / PRO+ / ULTRA, which determine the monthly grant.

When the balance drops below 50 credits, the model picker and account page warn you.

docs.title: Reading the prices
docs.text:
Each built-in model shows a price such as 0.9 / 2.7 — input and output respectively.

The unit is credits per thousand tokens. So 0.9 / 2.7 means 0.9 credits per thousand input tokens and 2.7 per thousand output tokens — that is 900 / 2700 credits per million tokens.

docs.title: Checking usage
docs.text:
Settings → Account, or Account & usage in the avatar menu:

  • Current balance, with the two buckets shown separately
  • This month's consumption
  • Consumption ranked by model

The per-day trend is not on the desktop account page — follow the top-up link to the web console and open its usage page.

docs.title: Topping up
docs.text: The top-up entry on the account page opens the web wallet. Redemption codes also work.

docs.title: Billing errors
docs.text:
When an AI call fails for a billing reason, you get a specific type and a matching action:

Message Meaning What to do Insufficient credits Not enough balance for this call Top up, or switch to your own model Quota exhausted The period's quota is used up Wait for the next period, or top up Rate limited You hit a frequency limit Wait a moment and retry Model not priced That model has no pricing yet Pick another model Model not allowed Your tier doesn't include it Switch model or upgrade No upstream channel No channel is currently available for that model Retry later or switch model Account suspended Account state problem Contact us

docs.title: Offline and degraded operation
docs.text: If the cloud is unreachable the app does not lock up: your local identity still shows, the balance and usage cards on the account page fall back to placeholders, and building, flashing, debugging and serial all keep working. Only conversations with built-in models are affected.

docs.title: Moving to another machine
docs.text: The account lives in the cloud. Install on the new machine, sign in with the same account, and your credits and usage come with it.

docs.title: AI Assistant
docs.text:
A docked panel on the right, toggled with Ctrl+J. Switching views does not interrupt the conversation.

It is not just a chat box: around 130 tools let it genuinely read and write files, build and flash, set breakpoints and step, read registers, configure pins and query Git.

docs.title: Choosing a model
docs.text: Settings → AI models, in two groups:

docs.title: Built-in
docs.text:
Works out of the box, no API key needed. Runs through the EmbAI cloud and is billed in credits; each model shows its price (e.g. 0.9 / 2.7, input and output respectively).

For how credits work, see Account & Credits.

docs.title: Your own models
docs.text:
Supply your own endpoint and API key. These go directly to the vendor and consume no EmbAI credits.

Supported vendors: Anthropic, OpenAI, Qwen, Zhipu GLM, MiniMax, Kimi (Moonshot), DeepSeek, and custom. The wire format can be responses, chat_completions or anthropic_messages.

API keys are stored encrypted, per account.

You can have both

Use the built-in models for convenience day to day, and switch to your own key for long runs. The model picker sits in the toolbar below the input box (left of the send button, showing the current model name), not at the top of the panel.

docs.title: Plan mode
docs.text:
Makes the AI submit a plan and wait for approval before acting. Worth it whenever the change is broad and you don't want it charging ahead.

Three ways to turn it on:

  • + to the left of the input → Plan mode
  • Type /plan <your task>
  • Ctrl+Alt+P

The input box then shows a blue outline and a lightbulb marker.

The AI produces a Markdown plan card, and you can:

Action Effect Approve Start executing the plan Request changes Send your comments back and have the plan revised Reject Turn the plan down Cancel Abort

The card's status follows execution (in progress, completed, incomplete, and so on).

⋯ in the panel header → Plan history and templates lets you review past plans, save good ones as reusable templates, and take checkpoints or roll back.

docs.title: Approval modes
docs.text:
The shield icon above the input decides when the AI must ask before acting:

Mode Behaviour Ask for approval File writes and risky operations always prompt Approve for me (default) Only operations judged risky prompt Full access Never prompts; may edit project files and flash directly (switching asks for confirmation)

Settings → AI models also has per-category tool switches: file operations, build, debug control, memory, trace analysis, hardware control, MCU configuration (peripheral and register access belongs here), SDK management, virtual hardware, toolchain, schematics, datasheets and promote-to-hardware, plus a few that are not localised yet and show their raw key (standard / knowledge / search / symbol / git / dashboard). Turning a category off removes those tools entirely.

The list is served dynamically by the backend, so new categories appear automatically.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text:
+ to the left of the input → Add:

  • File — pick from the project tree
  • Selected code — whatever is selected in the editor
  • Build errors — attach the errors from the build output directly
  • Image — screenshots, photos of the board, scope captures

docs.title: @ references
docs.text:
Typing @ triggers completion:

  • @schematic:filename — reference an analysed schematic
  • @datasheet:filename — reference an indexed datasheet

For example: "initialise SPI2 the way @schematic:mainboard-v2 wires it".

docs.title: Slash commands
docs.text: Command Purpose /plan <task> Start in Plan mode /template Use a plan template /explain Explain the selected or named code /fix Fix a problem /build Ask the AI to review the build configuration (not the same as the toolbar's Build) /flash Flash /register <name> Look up a register /peripheral <name> Look up a peripheral /hal <name> Generate HAL driver code for that peripheral

docs.title: When the AI asks you
docs.text: When a requirement is ambiguous the AI asks, offering two to four options to pick from rather than guessing. Code generation after project creation leans on this heavily — it walks through your requirements one item at a time.

docs.title: Session management
docs.text:
Action How New session Ctrl+L Stop the current answer Esc Focus the input Ctrl+K Archive / restore Toggle show-archived-tasks at the bottom of the session list Fork Copy the task from its current progress into a new thread; the original is kept in full (you cannot pick a past message as the fork point) Rewind Return to an earlier state and retry Compact context Summarise earlier turns to free up context Copy as Markdown Export the whole conversation

Conversations keep running in the background — closing the panel or switching views does not interrupt them, and the full transcript is there when you come back.

docs.title: Web search
docs.text: The AI can only search the web once you configure a search provider and key under Settings → AI models → Web search. Without it, it simply doesn't go online; nothing else is affected.

docs.title: Suggestions
docs.text:
• Use Plan mode for anything large — reading a plan is cheaper than rolling back
  • Hand it errors directly — + → Build errors beats paraphrasing them
  • Upload the schematic first — every later pin-related conversation gets shorter
  • Keep an eye on credits during long runs — built-in models bill per token, see Account & Credits

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
Press Build in the toolbar. In order:

  1. All unsaved tabs are saved automatically
  2. The bottom panel switches to Build output
  3. Keil's UV4.exe compiles the project
  4. The log streams in live, ending with N Error(s), M Warning(s)

Clean rebuild deletes the build/ directory first and compiles from scratch — useful when you suspect the incremental build.

Why Keil only

Projects EmbAI creates or imports are ordinary Keil projects (.uvprojx), and building hands off to UV4.exe. The output is therefore identical to compiling by hand in Keil, and colleagues without EmbAI can still open the project.

docs.title: Two reasons a build is refused
docs.text: Message Meaning 请先打开项目 No project is currently open Firmware library not ready HAL/CMSIS is still downloading. Wait, or press Retry in the status bar

docs.title: Compiler not found
docs.text:
未找到 Keil UV4.exe。请在「环境检测」中配置 Keil 路径，
或设置 KEIL_PATH 环境变量 / 在 .embai/config.json 写入 keil_path。

See Install & Setup.

docs.title: When the build fails
docs.text: The AI can read the build output directly. Say "fix the build errors" in the AI panel and it will read the log, locate the file and propose a fix.

docs.title: Flashing
docs.text:
With the probe and board connected, press Flash (existing firmware) or Build & flash (compile first).

A progress dialog walks through erase → program → verify. On success it offers an Open serial port button so you can go straight to the output.

docs.title: Automatic connection
docs.text:
If the probe isn't connected yet, EmbAI connects once automatically:

  • Target comes from the project's chip setting
  • Interface defaults to SWD, speed to 4000 kHz

docs.title: Common failures
docs.text:
Message Cause 未找到固件，请先构建项目 Nothing has been built successfully yet 自动连接失败: … No power, wrong wiring, locked debug port, or unsuitable interface/speed

J-Link's interface, speed and reset type can be changed from the J-Link indicator in the toolbar.

docs.title: The four flashing paths
docs.text:
J-LinkST-LinkDAPLink / CMSIS-DAPSerial ISP

The default. Requires the SEGGER driver pack. Progress is reported per phase.

Driven through OpenOCD, which must be on your PATH. Covers F0/F1/F2/F3/F4/F7/G0/G4/H7/ L0/L1/L4/L5/U5/WB/WL.

Not available in release builds — the pyocd package it depends on is not shipped with the installer, so connecting fails with pyocd not available. See Install & Setup.

The fallback when there is no debug probe: flashing over the serial bootloader.

The probe type can only be chosen in step 5 of the new-project wizard; there is no way to change it from inside the application afterwards, and the J-Link indicator in the toolbar opens J-Link's own parameters.

Flashing and debugging always go through J-Link today

The probe chosen in the wizard only affects the generated project configuration. To flash over ST-Link or DAPLink, use those vendors' own tools for the time being.

docs.title: Map file analysis
docs.text:
Activity bar → Build analysis → Map file analysis.

Parses the map file produced by the build and breaks Flash and RAM usage down by module and symbol — for answering "what exactly is eating my memory".

docs.title: Working with the AI
docs.text:
All of these can just be asked for:

  • "compile this" / "clean rebuild"
  • "build and flash it to the board"
  • "how much Flash are we using now"

Whether the AI has to ask permission first depends on the approval mode.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text: Activity bar → Core → Debug.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: Area Contents Top toolbar Start / Continue / Pause / Stop / Step in / Step over / Step out / Reset, plus settings entry points Left column Project files, variable watch, breakpoint list, call stack, power control Centre Source view — click the gutter to set breakpoints; the current line is marked

docs.title: Starting and stopping
docs.text:
With the board connected and firmware flashed, press Start debugging.

While disconnected the toolbar also offers a Hot Plug checkbox, for attaching to an already-running target without resetting it.

Once connected the toolbar switches to run control:

Button Effect Continue Run at full speed from the current position Pause Halt at the current PC Step in / over / out Single-step into a call, across it, or out to the caller Reset Reset the target Stop End the debug session

docs.title: Breakpoints
docs.text:
• Set one: click the gutter to the left of the source
  • Breakpoint list: the left column lists them all; click the dot on a row to enable/disable
  • Delete / edit: use the toolbar's Breakpoints / Watchpoints panel to delete, set conditions and see hit counts; clicking the same gutter line again also removes the breakpoint
  • Watchpoints: set data breakpoints from the breakpoint manager to halt on variable access

docs.title: Inspecting state
docs.text:
VariablesCall stackRegistersMemoryExpression evaluation

The Variables panel shows the locals of the function you are halted in (name / value / type), refreshed on every halt or step. Custom watch expressions are not supported yet — use expression evaluation in the toolbar for globals or a specific address.

The call chain when halted (function name + file:line), current frame at the top.

Read-only for now: clicking a frame does not jump to the source, and the variables panel always shows the frame at the current PC — you cannot switch to a caller's variables yet.

Live core register values.

There is no dedicated memory panel. To read memory by address, use the toolbar's command window and type mem read <addr> [<len>] (16 bytes if the length is omitted) — handy for peripheral registers or buffers.

The command window only allows reads; memory-write commands are rejected by an allow-list.

The expression panel evaluates an expression ad hoc — global variable names (once symbols are loaded) and 0x hex addresses are supported.

docs.title: Disassembly and symbols
docs.text: Disassembly is available, as is jumping to a symbol's definition from the toolbar's symbol navigation entry.

docs.title: Target power control
docs.text: The left column can turn target power on, off, or power-cycle it on probes that support it — a way to reset the supply without unplugging anything.

docs.title: Debug commands
docs.text: The command window in the toolbar lets you issue debug commands directly, which covers operations that have no dedicated button.

docs.title: Saving and restoring a session
docs.text: Debug configuration (breakpoints, watchpoints, Monitor mode) can be saved and restored, so you don't have to set everything up again next time.

docs.title: Monitor mode
docs.text:
The Monitor mode dialog in the toolbar switches between two ways of halting on a breakpoint: in Halt mode the CPU stops completely (the standard behaviour); in Monitor mode only the application thread is paused while interrupts and DMA keep running, which suits motor control and communication protocols. Not every Cortex-M part and probe supports Monitor mode.

Note

Switches labelled as UI placeholders in that dialog currently have no effect.

docs.title: RTT log
docs.text: The RTT log tab in the bottom panel receives SEGGER RTT output — useful for logging without occupying a UART.

docs.title: Working with the AI
docs.text:
The AI has the full set of debug control tools, so you can simply say:

  • "set a breakpoint at line 120 of main.c and start debugging"
  • "what's adc_value right now"
  • "read 32 bytes starting at 0x40020000"

Whether hardware operations require your confirmation depends on the approval mode.

docs.title: Editor
docs.text: Activity bar → Core → Editor. File tree on the left, tabbed editing area on the right.

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text:
These are the shortcuts the application actually binds.

Some entries in the in-app shortcut panel are placeholders

Ctrl+N (new file), Ctrl+O (open project), Ctrl+Shift+S (save all) and Ctrl+, (settings) are listed in that panel but are not wired up — pressing them does nothing. Only the working ones are listed below.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
Action Shortcut Quick open by filename Ctrl+P Save Ctrl+S

These have no shortcut; use the UI instead:

  • New file / folder — right-click a directory in the file tree
  • Open project — the project-name dropdown in the toolbar, or the welcome screen
  • Settings — the gear icon at the top right

docs.title: Editing and view
docs.text: Action Shortcut Undo / Redo Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z Find / Replace Ctrl+F / Ctrl+H Global search Ctrl+Shift+F Toggle sidebar Ctrl+B Split editor Ctrl+\ Toggle comment Ctrl+/

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text: Action Shortcut Back / Forward (previous, next location) Alt+Left / Alt+Right Go to definition F12 Symbol search Ctrl+T Close tab Ctrl+W Reopen closed tab Ctrl+Shift+T

docs.title: AI
docs.text:
Action Shortcut Show / hide the AI assistant Ctrl+J Focus the input box Ctrl+K New session Ctrl+L Toggle Plan mode Ctrl+Alt+P Stop the current answer Esc Inline AI chat (with code selected) Ctrl+I

Ctrl+B is not Build

It toggles the sidebar, as in VS Code. Build from the toolbar, or just ask the AI to compile.

docs.title: File tree
docs.text:
Shows the project directory. Right-click a file or folder to create a file, create a folder, rename or delete. (Drag-and-drop moving is not supported yet — rename, or move the file outside the app and refresh.)

There is no directory-level write protection

Vendor directories such as ARM/System, Drivers and FW can be edited and saved like any other file, and the tree shows no read-only marker. Take care not to edit HAL sources by accident.

"Vendor directories are read-only" is a convention for the AI assistant, not editor write protection: layered skeleton projects created by EmbAI record vendor_dirs_readonly in .embai/config.json and the AI is told not to touch them. Projects migrated from Keil don't get that field, but the AI is likewise told to confirm with you before changing vendor libraries.

docs.title: Tabs and splitting
docs.text: Ctrl+\ splits the editor so you can compare two files side by side. Ctrl+W closes the current tab and Ctrl+Shift+T brings it back.

docs.title: Global search
docs.text: Ctrl+Shift+F opens the search panel for project-wide text search with file filtering.

docs.title: Symbol navigation
docs.text: F12 jumps to a definition; Ctrl+T searches by symbol name. Alt+Left returns to where you were.

docs.title: Inline AI chat
docs.text:
Select a block of code in the editor, then press Ctrl+I (or pick "Inline Chat" from the context menu). An input box appears above the selection, letting you make a request about just that code ("switch this to DMA", "add error handling").

Selecting code alone does not open it — the shortcut or context menu is required.

  • Tab accepts the change
  • Esc discards it

This path does not consume the session in the right-hand AI panel, which makes it good for small edits. For larger changes prefer the AI panel, where you can watch the tool calls.

docs.title: Save-conflict protection
docs.text:
If a file has been edited in the editor while something else (Keil, or the AI) also changed it on disk, saving detects the conflict and warns instead of overwriting.

The same applies to building: pressing Build first saves all unsaved tabs, and if a conflict shows up the build is aborted with a prompt — so you never compile stale code by accident.

docs.title: Editor preferences
docs.text:
Theme and editor font size live under Settings → General (which also has language, autosave interval, file encoding and system notifications).

Line numbers, tab size, word wrap and the minimap belong to "Editor preferences", a panel that currently has no UI entry point.

docs.title: Creating a project
docs.text: From New project on the welcome screen, or New in the toolbar. Six steps:

docs.title: 1. Chip
docs.text: Filter by series or search a part number. 787 STM32 parts across 18 series.

docs.title: 2. Firmware library
docs.text:
Option Notes HAL ST's hardware abstraction layer — quick to start with, more code LL Low-layer, close to the registers, minimal overhead HAL + LL Both, so you can pick per peripheral SPL Standard Peripheral Library, for continuity with older projects

You can pin a specific Cube package version, or take the recommended one.

docs.title: 3. RTOS
docs.text: Bare metal / FreeRTOS / RT-Thread / CMSIS-RTOS. Choosing an RTOS lets you go on to set heap size, tick rate, memory scheme and priority count.

docs.title: 4. Peripherals & middleware
docs.text: UART, SPI, I²C, TIM, ADC and DMA, each configured individually. What you pick here shapes the generated initialisation code.

docs.title: 5. Toolchain & probe
docs.text: Defaults to Keil MDK + J-Link + SWD + 4000 kHz. Keil is currently the only supported firmware toolchain.

docs.title: 6. Name & location
docs.text:
Project name and directory, plus checkboxes for sample code, Git init (on by default), a unit test scaffold and Doxygen comments.

If Git isn't installed

"Git init" is skipped silently. Project creation is unaffected.

docs.title: After the wizard: wait, then hand over to the AI
docs.text:
Two things happen:

One — the firmware library downloads. EmbAI pulls the matching HAL/CMSIS sources from the STM32Cube repositories on GitHub, with progress in the status bar. You cannot build until it finishes — trying is blocked with a "firmware library not ready" message. On failure the status bar offers Retry.

Two — the AI takes over the firmware. The wizard only produces a skeleton that compiles. Once the project exists the AI panel opens and starts asking what you actually need, then writes the code file by file.

This is the intended workflow: the wizard does the bones, the AI does the flesh. You do not start from an empty main.c.

Generated structure varies by chip

The STM32H743 series uses a fixed layered Keil skeleton (ARM/ App/ HW/ FW/ Drivers/ Project). Other parts go through code generation and end up with a different structure — still a directly buildable Keil project.

docs.title: Opening an existing project
docs.text: Open project on the welcome screen, or the entry in the project-name dropdown. Select the project root. The dropdown also lets you open by typing a path.

docs.title: Migrating an existing Keil project
docs.text:
To bring an existing .uvprojx project into EmbAI: project-name dropdown → Migrate / import Keil project. Five steps:

  1. Detect — scans structure, part number, firmware library and include paths. Read-only; nothing is written
  2. Confirm — review what was detected and correct anything wrong
  3. Fill gaps — add missing HAL/CMSIS pieces
  4. Test build — compile once to prove the import still builds
  5. Done

Afterwards the AI introduces the project's structure to you, so you can start making requests straight away.

docs.title: Recent projects
docs.text: The welcome screen lists recently opened projects with search, ordering and removal. The last project is restored automatically on the next launch, along with the editor tabs you had open.

docs.title: The project configuration file
docs.text:
Every project has an .embai/ directory whose config.json records the wizard's choices:

Field Meaning chip / series Part number and series name Project name firmware_lib hal / ll / hal-ll / spl toolchain Currently always keil-mdk debugger Debug probe rtos / middleware RTOS and middleware choices peripherals Peripheral configuration layout Project layout type keil_path Optional override for the UV4.exe used by this project

It is safe to commit — a colleague who clones the repo gets the same configuration.

docs.title: Making new projects follow your team's conventions
docs.text: If you have uploaded and activated a coding standard under Coding standard, the AI will follow it when creating projects — directory layout, file headers, naming and peripheral initialisation order.

docs.title: Schematics & Knowledge
docs.text: Teach the AI what your board looks like and how your team writes code. Once that is set up, a lot of explaining stops being necessary.

docs.title: Schematics
docs.text: Activity bar → Virtual & schematics → Schematics.

docs.title: Uploading and analysis
docs.text:
PDFs and images are both accepted. After uploading, start the analysis and the AI reads the whole sheet visually. The process is visible — a timeline lights up each block as it is recognised, rather than a spinner hiding a black box.

Results are split across seven tabs:

Tab Contents MCU pins MCU pin ↔ peripheral/net correspondence, accepted or rejected row by row Components The component list Nets Net connectivity Blocks The functional blocks it identified Function / firmware What each block is, which MCU peripheral and pins it uses, how to initialise it — reading a schematic is ultimately about writing firmware, and this is the most useful tab Past analyses Append-only record of previous analyses Raw text The raw text the vision model extracted

docs.title: When recognition is off
docs.text: Schematics usually cram a lot onto one sheet, so whole-page recognition is never perfect. You can re-crop the region you care about and analyse just that — accuracy improves noticeably.

docs.title: Referencing it in chat
docs.text:
Once analysis is complete, typing @ completes to @schematic:filename. For example:

Initialise SPI2 and that ST7789 the way @schematic:mainboard-v2 wires them

The AI reads the structured result instead of making you type pin numbers.

docs.title: Project knowledge base
docs.text:
Activity bar → Virtual & schematics → Project knowledge base. Three columns:

  • Left — schematics, datasheets and reference material
  • Centre — the parsing notes for a selected schematic
  • Right — the structured analysis, or a datasheet's indexing status

Selecting an entry lets you open a dedicated AI session: a schematic gets a multimodal analysis, a datasheet gets an explanation of its key registers and initialisation sequence with page citations, and selecting nothing produces an overview of the whole knowledge base.

docs.title: Datasheet Q&A
docs.text:
Datasheets in the project knowledge base are chunked and indexed, after which you can reference them with @datasheet:filename or simply ask "what does bit 3 of this register do" — answers cite the page they came from.

The right-hand column can re-index a datasheet (enabling vector retrieval), which is worth trying when retrieval quality is poor.

There is currently no dedicated datasheet upload button

What the UI can upload is schematics and coding standards. Datasheets can be indexed and queried once they appear in the knowledge base list.

docs.title: Coding standard
docs.text:
Activity bar → Virtual & schematics → Coding standard.

Upload your team's coding-standard document (.md / .txt / .pdf / .docx) and the AI distils it into a structured profile: directory layout, file-header template, naming rules, formatting conventions, peripheral initialisation order and so on.

Once you press Activate:

  • New projects are laid out and generated according to that standard
  • Day-to-day code generation follows the same conventions

This is the most direct way to get output that looks like your team wrote it rather than like it came out of a tutorial.

docs.title: A suggested setup order
docs.text:
When you pick up a new board, ten minutes spent like this pays off:

  1. Upload the schematic, analyse it, and check the pin mapping came out right
  2. Make sure the relevant datasheet is in the knowledge base
  3. If your team has a standards document, upload it and activate it

Start making requests after that and the quality of what you get back is noticeably different.

docs.title: Serial & Dashboard
docs.text:
EmbAI has two serial interfaces for different jobs:

Use for Serial terminal (bottom panel) Sending and receiving text, reading logs, issuing debug commands Serial dashboard (activity bar) Plotting the numbers coming over the port in real time

docs.title: Serial terminal
docs.text: Bottom panel → Serial terminal. The Serial indicator in the toolbar also connects and disconnects directly.

docs.title: Connection parameters
docs.text: Parameter Values Baud rate Dropdown only — 22 fixed rates from 1200 to 4000000 (default 115200); custom values are not supported Data bits 5 / 6 / 7 / 8 Stop bits 1 / 1.5 / 2 Parity None / Odd / Even Reset on open Resets the target when the port opens

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• HEX view — show incoming bytes as hexadecimal
  • Timestamps — prefix each line with its arrival time
  • RX / TX byte counters
  • CJK re-decoding — recovers text when firmware emits GBK-encoded characters
  • History — recall and resend previous commands

docs.title: Serial dashboard
docs.text:
Activity bar → Serial → Serial dashboard.

A drag-and-drop dashboard: bind values from the serial stream to widgets and watch them live.

docs.title: Widgets
docs.text:
Widget Use Waveform Time-series curves for one or more channels Gauge Circular needle gauge Number Large numeric readout Indicator Boolean state Slider Drag to send a value down to the device Button Send a preset command on click Terminal Embedded text send/receive

The toolbar has Add widget, Protocol / channels, Edit layout (drag and resize) and Export CSV.

Layouts are stored in the project's .embai/dashboard.json, so they can be committed alongside the code.

docs.title: Data protocols
docs.text: Protocol Notes FireWater Text format, name:value JustFloat Binary float frames with a frame tail RawData Raw bytes, interpreted per your own convention None No parsing

docs.title: Auto-detection
docs.text:
After connecting, EmbAI tries to identify the data format. When it does, a banner appears along the lines of "detected probable protocol X (N channels, confidence M%)", which you can apply or ignore.

This saves counting channels by hand — most of the time applying it gets you straight to a working plot.

docs.title: A typical session
docs.text:
1. Have the firmware emit a few variables in JustFloat or FireWater format
  2. Open the dashboard, connect, and apply the auto-detection banner when it appears
  3. Add widget → Waveform → bind the channels
  4. Add a slider if you want to tune a parameter live
  5. Export CSV when you need a record

docs.title: Working with the AI
docs.text:
The AI can drive both the port and the dashboard:

  • "connect the serial port at 115200"
  • "add a waveform showing channels 1 and 2"
  • "read the recent serial output and tell me what you make of it"

docs.title: Virtual Display
docs.text:
Activity bar → Virtual & schematics → Virtual display.

The tiresome part of bringing up an OLED or TFT UI is the loop: change a line, compile, flash, look, change another line. The virtual display collapses that to seconds — your driver code is compiled and run on your PC, the bytes it writes to SPI/I²C are intercepted, replayed through a real controller model, and rendered straight into the view.

No board, no flashing.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
You need a host CMake and GCC — note that this is your PC's native compiler, not an Arm cross toolchain.

When they are missing a banner appears at the top of the view.

Install the toolchain by hand

The one-click installer downloads and unpacks a toolchain, but its bundled checksums are placeholders, so integrity verification is skipped entirely — whatever is downloaded gets installed unverified. Install CMake and MinGW-w64 / LLVM-mingw yourself, put them on PATH, and reopen the view.

docs.title: Supported panels
docs.text:
22 controllers, covering monochrome OLEDs, colour TFTs, round displays and AMOLEDs:

Category Models Monochrome OLED SSD1306 (I²C / SPI), SH1106 Colour TFT ST7789 (240×240 / 240×320 / 240×280 / 135×240), ILI9341, ST7735 (128×160 / 128×128), ILI9488, ST7796, SSD1351 Round GC9A01, CO5300 (360 / 466), SH8601 (454 / 368×448) Other RM67162, SSD1963 (800×480 / 480×272), NT35510

Pick a model from the dropdown at the top and the canvas takes on that panel's resolution and shape.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
1. Put your driver and UI code in the project's virtual_ui/ directory (failing that, a virtual_main.c in the project root)
  2. Select the panel model
  3. Press Build & run
  4. The picture appears on the canvas; the build/run log at the bottom shows the output

The toolbar also has stop, reset, screenshot, and 1× / 2× / 4× / 8× zoom.

docs.title: Simulated input
docs.text:
The right-hand column injects input into the running program:

Panel Purpose Buttons Simulate key press and release Potentiometer Drag a slider to inject an ADC voltage Serial monitor Watch what the program prints to the virtual UART (read-only; sending data is not supported yet)

Turn on Mouse touch in the toolbar and clicks on the canvas are injected as touch events — so touchscreen UIs can be exercised directly.

docs.title: Promote to hardware
docs.text:
Once the UI looks right, press Promote to hardware to turn the virtual project into real firmware code.

Two steps:

  1. Preview — a dry run listing the files that would be added or changed, the pin mapping, the bus mapping and any warnings. You tick which ones to take
  2. Apply — only then is anything written to disk

If a target file has been edited by hand it is flagged as a conflict rather than silently overwritten; you can explicitly opt into overwriting when that is what you want.

docs.title: Working with the AI
docs.text:
The AI can start and stop virtual runs, take screenshots of the current frame, inject buttons and ADC values, and read the virtual serial port. So you can say:

  • "run the virtual display and screenshot what it looks like"
  • "set the potentiometer to 1.5 V and take another shot"
  • "the main screen isn't centred properly — run it yourself, look, and fix it"

The point of this path is that the AI can see the UI it wrote and iterate on its own, instead of using you as its eyes every time.
